title: Sophie Tucker, Lady Mountbatten and the invitation to London
summary: After a visit by Sophie Tucker, the band gets booked to London in 1933.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: How was the -- how did it come about that you all decided to go to Europe.
Oh, that's a good question. You know, Sophie Tucker, You heard of Sophie?

She was big, so one night she come up there with Lady Mountbatten, Lord Louis Mountbatten was a big man, an Englishman, he was Lord Louis Mountbatten. During the war he was in charge of a whole fleet, so he was a big man, one of the biggest and she was a cousin of the Queen, Lady Mountbatten was.

So Sophie, she was visiting in the United States and she was a friend of Sophie Tucker, because Sophie had played in Europe, and Sophie had brought her up because when you come to New York, if you didn't go to the Cotton Club, you hadn't seen New York, so she brought her to the Cotton Club.
We didn't know nothing about no Lord or Lady

Mountbatten so Sophie Tucker came over as soon as she come in, they introduced her, Miss Tucker's in the house. We played "Some of These Days." That was her big number then, written by this colored cat. I forget his name -- Shelton -- Shelton Thomas, he wrote that tune, and gave it to her and it made her famous, because she always mentioned it.

So we played her theme song, and then we went through our repertoire playing different numbers, so during the intermission she come backstage and go Duke, said Duke, I want you to meet some friends of mine so we could socialize all over the place, so Duke went out and met her and so she said, "Oh, I never heard no band like that. What do you call it the Cotton Club orchestra?" We did, you know, she said, "Oh, no, she said, if it were left to me I would call it the Aristocrats of Jazz." That's how we changed our name. Duke Ellington and the Aristocrats of Jazz.

So she said, "How would you like to come to London?" So Duke told her you could play all over Europe but no American bands played in London. You remember that, no American bands were allowed to play in London, so Duke said -- he still don't know who she is, so later on, that's Lady Mountbatten -- so she said, "Would you come to London? I would like for you to come to London. My people could hear you." So Duke said, "Oh, that would be fine."
Now, this was in 1933, about April or something like
that. She said, I'll fix it for you, so sure enough she did, and she come back up there about a couple weeks later and said it's all finished, it's all arranged, so that's how we come to London.
Wasn't no American band was allowed you could play in Paris, France and all over, but London, I don't know what -- one of them dumb ideas, no Americans, could play in London. You could play in Paris.
